title: Polymers and Plastics

cards.h: The material of the modern age
cards.b: Your clothes, bottle, phone case, pipes, car tyres and even DNA are polymers: giant molecules made by joining thousands of small units (monomers). Plastics changed the world, and now trouble it.

Like paper clips chained together, many small molecules link into a long chain. The repeating chain is written (-unit-)n, where n can be in thousands.

Natural polymers: cellulose, starch, proteins, natural rubber, DNA. Synthetic ones: polythene, nylon, PVC, polyester.

Monomers with a C=C double bond open up and join end to end. No by-product.

n CH2=CH2 → (-CH2-CH2-)n polythene (polyethene).

Other examples: PVC from vinyl chloride, polystyrene, Teflon (PTFE) from tetrafluoroethene, polypropene.

Monomers join and release a small molecule, usually water.

  • Nylon-6,6: made by Wallace Carothers at DuPont (1935) from a diamine and a diacid, joined by amide links.
  • Polyester (PET): diol + diacid, joined by ester links; the plastic of water bottles and fabrics.
  • Bakelite (Leo Baekeland, 1907): first fully synthetic plastic, from phenol and formaldehyde.

• Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded: polythene, PVC, PET. Recyclable.
  • Thermosets set permanently with cross-links: Bakelite, melamine, epoxy. They char rather than melt.

Rubber: Charles Goodyear (1839) discovered vulcanisation, heating rubber with sulphur to form cross-links, making it strong and elastic.

Most plastics are chemically stable, so they last hundreds of years. Millions of tonnes reach oceans; larger pieces break into microplastics that enter food chains. Solutions: reduce, reuse, recycle, redesign. Biodegradable plastics (like PLA from starch) break down, but often only in industrial composters.

Ethene C2H4 has molar mass 2 x 12 + 4 = 28 g/mol. A polythene chain of 1,000 units has mass 1,000 x 28 = 28,000 g/mol.

Addition: monomers in = polymer out, no loss: 56 g of ethene makes 56 g polythene. Condensation loses water: each amide link formed releases one H2O (18 g/mol).

• Biodegradable does not mean it vanishes anywhere; conditions matter.
  • Recycling codes (1 to 7) identify type; the arrow symbol does not guarantee that it is recycled.
  • Nylon is not natural silk. It was marketed as 'synthetic silk' in the 1930s.
  • Plastic is not one substance but a huge family.

India's Plastic Waste Management Rules (2016, amended since) set producer responsibility, and a ban on identified single-use plastic items took effect on 1 July 2022. India is a major producer of polyester and PET, with Reliance among large producers. Natural-fibre alternatives like jute, a cellulose polymer from Bengal, offer biodegradable bags.

• Polymers are long chains of repeating monomers.
  • Addition: n CH2=CH2 → polythene. Condensation: loses water, e.g. nylon, PET.
  • Thermoplastics remould; thermosets do not. Vulcanisation cross-links rubber.
